A 33-year-old man seeks medical attention for worsening cough, increased sputum production, and
recent onset dyspnea. He has no significant medical history except for a 10 pack-year smoking history
and takes only a daily multivitamin. His vital signs show: | Temperature | 38.7°C (101.6°F) | | --- | --- | |
Blood pressure | 128/88 mm Hg | | Heart rate | 82/min | | Respiratory rate | 24/min | | Oxygen saturation
| 93% on room air | Physical examination reveals bilateral crackles and decreased breath sounds at the
right posterior lung base. Osteopathic examination identifies a small, firm, painful nodule at the right
sternal border in the 4th intercostal space. After performing ligamentous articular strain technique on
bilateral Sibson's fascia, the physician plans an additional treatment to enhance lymphatic drainage
and alveolar opening. Which of the following describes the correct positioning for this treatment?
Answer Choices: (A) Patient lies prone; physician at the right side of the patient places bilateral thenar
eminences over the posterior surface of ribs 4–6 (B) Patient lies supine; physician at the right side of
the patient places bilateral thenar eminences over the anterior surface of ribs 4–6 (C) Patient lies
supine; physician at the head of the table places bilateral thenar eminences over the anterior surface of
ribs 1–3 (D) Patient lies prone; physician at the left side of the patient places bilateral thenar eminences
over the posterior surface of ribs 3–5 (E) Patient lies supine; physician at the head of the table places
bilateral thenar eminences over the anterior surface of ribs 2–4 (F) Patient lies supine; physician at the
head of the table places bilateral thenar eminences over the anterior surface of ribs 5–7 (G) Patient lies
prone; physician at the head of the table places bilateral thenar eminences over the posterior surface of
ribs 2–4 (H) Patient lies supine; physician at the foot of the table places bilateral thenar eminences over
the anterior surface of ribs 3–5 (I) Patient lies supine; physician at the left side of the patient places
bilateral thenar eminences over the anterior surface of ribs 5–7 (J) Patient lies supine; physician at the
right side of the patient places bilateral thenar eminences over the anterior surface of ribs 6–7
 A. Patient lies supine; physician at the head of the table places bilateral thenar eminences over the
anterior surface of ribs 2–4
B. Patient lies supine; physician at the foot of the table places bilateral thenar eminences over the
anterior surface of ribs 3–5
C. Patient lies supine; physician at the right side of the patient places bilateral thenar eminences
over the anterior surface of ribs 4–6
D. Patient lies supine; physician at the right side of the patient places bilateral thenar eminences
over the anterior surface of ribs 6–7
E. Patient lies prone; physician at the right side of the patient places bilateral thenar eminences over
the posterior surface of ribs 4–6
F. Patient lies supine; physician at the head of the table places bilateral thenar eminences over the
anterior surface of ribs 5–7

G. Patient lies prone; physician at the head of the table places bilateral thenar eminences over the
posterior surface of ribs 2–4
H. Patient lies prone; physician at the left side of the patient places bilateral thenar eminences over
the posterior surface of ribs 3–5
I. Patient lies supine; physician at the head of the table places bilateral thenar eminences over the
anterior surface of ribs 1–3
J. Patient lies supine; physician at the left side of the patient places bilateral thenar eminences over
the anterior surface of ribs 5–7
